items.passage: Three rules governed the wall between Kwesi's beekeeper's yard and Kwame's house in Dakar: no climbing, no smoke on windy days, and no talk of the photograph. Kwame kept the picture in a frame, a print of two boys on one bicycle beside a row of hives against that same wall, and each morning he hung it in his window facing the yard. Years ago Kwesi had moved his hives to the far corner, saying the bees disliked the afternoon heat by the wall, and he worked there with his back to the window. In the dry season of 1987, Kwame's son mentioned at the well that his father now read the newspaper with a glass and no longer crossed the street alone. That same week Kwesi began moving the hives back, one each evening after dark, telling anyone who asked that the far corner flooded in the rains. By March the last hive stood under the window, humming. Each morning Kwesi set a jar of the first honey on top of the wall, its lid loosened.

items.passage: Thessaloniki was still dark when Despina and I let ourselves into her uncle's bakery to practice, as we had every morning that winter, among the cooling racks. Flour on the music stand. Flour on the bow. Her uncle charged us nothing but the sweeping. A letter from the conservatory in Vienna lay folded inside her violin case, offering one place, for one player, beginning in March. We played the second movement and stopped at the bar where we always stopped. She tuned her A string. I tuned mine. Outside, the first cart came for the bread, and the driver whistled our opening phrase, badly, as he did most days. When we finished, I swept from the ovens to the door, then went back and swept the corner beneath her chair a second time, where there was nothing left to sweep, and set her case by the door with the clasp already fastened.

items.passage: Two herrings on Mondays, a smoked eel on Thursdays, and no credit: those were the terms Herr Gyeongho set when Katharina first came to his stall at the edge of the omnibus depot in Hamburg. She called him Herr Gyeongho, he called her Fraulein, and they bargained each week over a pfennig as if the stall depended on it. In the winter her mother's wages from the depot laundry stopped. Katharina still came on Mondays and Thursdays and paid what she could, and he wrapped the fish and dropped the coins into his apron without looking at them. Some weeks he complained loudly to the tram drivers that business was poor. One afternoon, sent to fetch paper from under his counter, she opened the wrong drawer and found a ledger in her own family's name, page after page of small sums, every line crossed through in the same blue pencil. She closed the drawer. The next Monday she set a pfennig more than the price on the scale before he could speak, and he let it lie there.

Tatiana, the youngest violinist, had joined at fifteen; she was nineteen now, and a quartet in Berlin had written to her twice. All week she arrived early, unpacked her violin, and left the case open on the chair beside her, its velvet lining turned toward the door. Irena watched her play the slow movement with her shoulders lifted, a swallow perched on a wire that hums. During rehearsals the others asked Tatiana to lead the tuning, and she did, every morning, before anyone else had taken a seat. items.passage: When my grandfather moved into our flat above the terraced gardens in Manila, he brought three suitcases and a Greek grammar for me. Stavros had decided I would learn his language by summer, and every evening on the terrace he drilled verbs while the neighbors' radios played. I complained to my friends that he taught like a drill sergeant with a cough. For my birthday he gave me a wool sweater, knitted by his sister in Thessaloniki, in a city where the evenings rarely drop below twenty-five degrees. I told him it was perfect. That was not a lie, exactly; it was a word I had just learned from him. On weekends I went out with friends and left the grammar under my bed. But I wore the sweater to every lesson on the terrace, sweating, until the cuffs stretched past my wrists. Years later the grammar sits on my desk with his pencil marks in the margins, and I still conjugate one verb aloud before I open the window.

items.passage: We kept a tailoring shop in Tehran on a street with too many tailors, and by the third winter our ledger ran mostly red. My brother Kemoy cut the cloth; I, Hemi, did the seams and the slow finishing. Every coat that left the shop carried a small linen tag in its collar, stitched with a single letter: K. When a colonel's wife admired a coat in the window, Kemoy thanked her at the counter while I sat in the back with pins in my mouth. That evening on the roof, where we hung the shop's linen to dry, I said a good deal. For a month afterward we pegged our cloths at opposite ends of the line. One coat came back for mending in February with its tag cut out, and neither of us asked who had done it. In March I went up to take in the new tags Kemoy had washed and starched. Each one read K. and H., the second letter in his clumsier hand. He came up behind me with the basket and pegged his shirts beside mine.

He had been my father's closest friend; he arrived with a rake and insisted the leaves be burned, and I insisted they be left to rot into the flower beds. My father had sailed for Fujian when I was nine. Baoyu asked after my schooling, my cough, the price of rice, and never once after him. We argued for six autumns, loudly enough that the neighbors leaned from their windows to listen. One year he set a small tin box on the fountain's rim while we shouted, and carried it home again when he left. The seventh October he did not come. A boy brought the rake and the tin box to our gate. Inside was a photograph of a young man in shirtsleeves raking leaves into that same basin, and on its back, in my father's hand, the year I was born. I leaned the rake against the fountain and left the leaves where they lay.

items.passage: Brine and coal smoke: that was the smell of the crossing on the salt flats east of Manchester, where my father ran the little ferry over the brine channel for thirty years. Each spring a passenger named Josiah bought two tickets and rode alone at the stern, hat in his hands, and left the second ticket tucked into the rail. My father punched both and never asked. The winter after my father died, the engine began to cough, and the yard at Irlam offered me three possible weeks in April for the overhaul. I took the second. Josiah's Tuesday fell in it; my father had chalked that date on the wheelhouse wall every year, and I had not washed it off. "Repairs," I said, when Josiah came down the path that morning. "Engine won't be ready till the summer trade." I untied my father's old skiff from the jetty, set the oars in their locks, and held the bow steady while he stepped in. On the far bank I took a ticket punch from my coat.

Smell of split guava, sweet and gone to vinegar,
the wasps loud in it. In March the deed changed hands;
Ximena paid the last wage in an envelope
and wrote the new gate code on its flap.

lifting what the wind brought down,

on the gatepost nail where anyone could take them,

### lit40-hard-03-081 — skill inferences · 유형 relationship_between_characters · 요청 난이도 hard · hard 기준: 관계의 방향(누가 누구에게 의존·양보하는가)을 읽어야 하고, 호칭이 주는 표면 관계가 가장 강한 오답으로 작동하며, 오답이 지문과 충돌하지 않는다

When the last crate of my father's records was sold, Ofelia counted the bills twice on the folding table between the lemon sellers and the fish stalls of the Valparaiso market. I had called her Señora all morning, as I called the woman who ran the bakery, and she answered to it. The plan had been hers: sell the records before the rent came due and keep me at the same school. A man in a striped scarf carried off the jazz albums; a student took the rest in two trips. Ofelia divided the bills into two stacks, slid the thicker one toward me, and said, "For the rent, Emiliano. Count it." The thinner one went into her apron. At the empanada cart she bought one, handed it to me, and said she had already eaten. On the walk uphill she carried the empty crates. That night the rent envelope on the kitchen table was thicker than the stack I had counted, and her apron hung on its hook, the pocket flat.

[질문] Based on the text, which choice best describes the relationship between Ofelia and Emiliano?
A) Emiliano keeps Ofelia at a formal distance, while she quietly bears costs on his behalf.
B) Emiliano treats Ofelia as a respected elder, while she accepts the formal role he gives.
C) Emiliano and Ofelia work as partners in a sale, while they split what their plan earns.
D) Emiliano helps Ofelia through a hard morning, while she relies on him to finish the sale.
### lit40-hard-03-084 — skill inferences · 유형 symbolism · 요청 난이도 hard · hard 기준: 사물이 두 맥락에서 다른 의미를 띠고, 가장 강한 오답이 인물 관계로 읽은 그럴듯한 상징 해석이다
[지문]
Four rules held in the tailor's back room, which Weiqi and I rented on alternate mornings that Vermont winter to proof our dough: no talk of prices, no borrowed flour, no opening the window, and nothing of mine crosses the chalk line on the floor. I had drawn that line myself, heel to heel across the boards, and each Monday I knelt and traced it fresh. Weiqi, whose bakery stood three doors from mine, kept to her side without comment. On a Thursday in February a letter came addressed to the tailor, and Weiqi opened it, thinking it was hers. The building would be sold in spring. She read it aloud to me anyway, from her side, and then we stood a long while among the rising bowls. The following Monday I knelt with the chalk in my hand, as always. My name is Matheus. I set the chalk back in its tin, and when Weiqi's bowl of rye needed the warmer corner, I lifted it across myself.

[질문] Based on the text, what does the chalk line most likely represent?
A) A practical rule that lets two tenants share a single rented room
B) Matheus's wish to guard his methods from a competing baker
C) A lost friendship between the bakers that the letter restores
D) A separation Matheus had insisted on, which he no longer keeps
### lit40-hard-03-086 — skill words_in_context · 유형 figurative_language · 요청 난이도 hard · hard 기준: 관용 해석으로 풀 수 없고, 오답이 비유의 다른 속성에서 나온 그럴듯한 해석이며 정답은 두 곳 이상의 단서가 정한다
[지문]
When the power failed across Old Dhaka, the night pharmacy where Tara worked became the only lit room on the lane, and by midnight two families had carried their festival trays to its single steel counter. Tara's aunt laid out rice pudding for Eid. Hari, who had sailed cargo ships for thirty years and now rented the room above the shop, came down with a brass plate of marigolds and sweets for his evening prayer. Three times he set it near the corner; three times, when an arm reached past him, he drew it back against his chest. Hari's plate stayed at the counter's rim, a skiff riding out the night beyond the harbor lights. Tara moved two bowls and left a space. He looked at it and held the plate level. Later her aunt spooned pudding onto a leaf, set it on the empty steel, and pushed it a finger's width toward him. The marigolds went into the middle, and his small lamp leaned toward the rice.

[질문] As used in the text, the phrase "a skiff riding out the night beyond the harbor lights" most nearly suggests that Hari
A) is weighed down by the plate he has carried for his evening prayer.
B) has fixed the counter's rim as a boundary he intends to keep.
C) is waiting outside the gathering until a place is offered to him.
D) is falling back on habits formed during his years on cargo ships.
### lit40-hard-03-087 — skill words_in_context · 유형 figurative_language · 요청 난이도 hard · hard 기준: 관용 해석으로 풀 수 없고, 오답이 비유의 다른 속성에서 나온 그럴듯한 해석이며 정답은 두 곳 이상의 단서가 정한다
[지문]
Years later I can still see Angus at the crossing below Kelvin Mill, where the burn had dried that August to a bed of grey stones. I clerked for him three mornings a week, long after he had left the bench; he called me Miss Maeve and nothing shorter. In his breast pocket he kept an envelope addressed, in his own hand, to a man he had once sentenced, and its corners had gone soft as cloth. Each morning at the near edge of the stones he pressed two fingers flat against that pocket, stood a while, and turned us toward the bridge. For him the letter was a ford walked daily toward a bank that never came nearer. I would wait with the satchel. On the last dry morning he went out as far as the middle, sat on a flat rock long enough to read a page, and came back with the pocket buttoned. We went round by the bridge, as before.

[질문] As used in the text, the phrase "a ford walked daily toward a bank that never came nearer" most nearly suggests that the letter is
A) a weight that presses on Angus each time he sets out in the morning.
B) a barrier that conditions outside Angus keep placing in his way.
C) a duty left from his years on the bench that still orders his days.
D) an effort Angus resumes each day without bringing it to an end.
### lit40-hard-03-088 — skill words_in_context · 유형 figurative_language · 요청 난이도 hard · hard 기준: 관용 해석으로 풀 수 없고, 오답이 비유의 다른 속성에서 나온 그럴듯한 해석이며 정답은 두 곳 이상의 단서가 정한다
[지문]
Smell of split guava, sweet and gone to vinegar,
the wasps loud in it. In March the deed changed hands;
Ximena paid the last wage in an envelope
and wrote the new gate code on its flap.
Still, each dawn, Kiara walks the rows above Kingston
lifting what the wind brought down,
binding cracked limbs to their stakes with green twine,
the same knot, the same three turns, tree after tree.
She moves among them, a candle trimmed for a ship already moored,
and the light comes up behind her over the Blue Mountains.
Ximena watches from the porch, her coffee going cold,
and says nothing of the clearing crew due in June.
At dusk Kiara rinses the twine knife at the cistern,
wipes it on her skirt, and hangs her ring of keys
on the gatepost nail where anyone could take them,
then walks down the hill toward the road.

[질문] As used in the text, the phrase "a candle trimmed for a ship already moored" most nearly suggests that Kiara's work is
A) a devotion she keeps up though no one now requires it of her.
B) a strength that is wearing away the longer she stays on.
C) a bid to be noticed and kept on by the orchard's new owner.
D) the plain habit of a worker used to rising before daylight.
### lit40-hard-03-089 — skill words_in_context · 유형 figurative_language · 요청 난이도 hard · hard 기준: 관용 해석으로 풀 수 없고, 오답이 비유의 다른 속성에서 나온 그럴듯한 해석이며 정답은 두 곳 이상의 단서가 정한다
[지문]
Rosedale, Mississippi, still keeps its salt-water pool, fed by a brackish well the town drilled in 1958 and never managed to sweeten. Aaliyah came back to survey the levee and found Darnell, the keeper, raking leaves off the surface as he had when she was ten. The water sat an inch lower on the tiles each year, he said, and each Sunday he ran the pump an hour to bring it back. She had left on a scholarship at seventeen, one of four the county gave that spring; on the honor board by the bathhouse, the other three names had addresses in Memphis and Chicago pencilled under them. In her notes that night she called the scholarship a sluice gate the town had opened for its own children. The next morning she measured the pool wall with her rod and logged the figure. Before she drove off, she ran the pump for an hour herself, though it was Tuesday.

[질문] As used in the text, the phrase "a sluice gate the town had opened for its own children" most nearly suggests that the scholarship was
A) a route to wider success that the town proudly offered to its youth.
B) an opening the town made itself that slowly let its young flow away.
C) a barrier that let the town decide which of its children could go.
D) a structure meant to manage the water that the levee holds back.
